arXiv:1403.4104v1 [math.AC] 17 Mar 2014

ENCODING ALGEBRAIC POWER SERIES

M.E.÷ ALONSO, F.J.÷ CASTRO-JIMÉNEZ, H.÷ HAUSER

††M.A.÷ acknowledges support from MEC, 2011-22435, and UCM, Grupo 910444; F.C.-J.÷ from MTM-2010-19336 and Feder; H.H.÷ from the Austrian Science Fund FWF, projects P-21461 and P-25652.

Abstract: The division algorithm for ideals of algebraic power series satisfying Hironaka’s box condition is shown to be finite when expressed suitably in terms of the defining polynomial codes of the series. In particular, the codes of the reduced standard basis of the ideal can be constructed effectively.

1. Introduction

Let H:𝔸Kn+p→𝔸KpH:{{{\tenmsb A}}}^{n+p}_{K}\rightarrow{{{\tenmsb A}}}^{p}_{K} be a polynomial map between affine spaces over a field KK. Assume that HH satisfies at 00 the assumption of the implicit function theorem,

∂yH⁡(0,0)∈Glp​(K)\partial_{y}H(0,0)\in{\rm Gl}_{p}(K) and H⁡(0,0)=0H(0,0)=0,

where y=(y1,…,yp)y=(y_{1},\ldots,y_{p}) denote coordinates on 𝔸Kp{{{\tenmsb A}}}^{p}_{K}. Then there is a unique formal power series solution h=(h1,…,hp)h=(h_{1},\ldots,h_{p}) of the system H⁡(x,y)=0H(x,y)=0 at 00, say

H⁡(x,h⁡(x))=0H(x,h(x))=0 and h⁡(0)=0h(0)=0.

Actually, the components hih_{i} are algebraic power series in the sense that each hih_{i} satisfies a univariate polynomial equation over the polynomial ring K⁡[x1,…,xn]K[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}]. Conversely, any algebraic power series h1h_{1} arises in this way: There is a system of polynomial equations H⁡(x,y)=0H(x,y)=0 satisfying the assumption of the implicit function theorem so that the unique solution hh has first component h1h_{1}. This is known as the Artin-Mazur theorem [AM, AMR, BCR]. The characterization allows one to encode algebraic power series by a polynomial vector H∈K​[x,y]pH\in K[x,y]^{p} as above. The advantage of this code in comparison with taking the minimal polynomial lies in the fact that the latter determines the algebraic series only up to conjugation, so that extra information is necessary to specify the series, typically a sufficiently high truncation of the Taylor expansion. In contrast, the polynomial code HH determines the series h1h_{1} completely and is easy to handle algebraically.

Phrased more abstractly, the henselization of the localization of K⁡[x1,…,xn]K[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}] at the maximal ideal (x1,…,xn)(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}) can be realized as the direct limit of finite étale extensions [Ar1, Na1, BCR, BrK]. Any element hh of the henselization, i.e., any algebraic power series, therefore belongs to such an extension – which, by definition, can be described by a code as above.

It is then natural to ask to what extent operations with algebraic power series can be expressed in terms of their code; and, if this is the case for a certain operation, what will be the respective formulation of the operation in terms of the code.

In the present article we answer this question for the division of algebraic power series and for the construction of reduced standard bases of ideals. When just considered for formal power series, the division is an infinite algorithm in the infinitely many coefficients of the series. If the involved series are algebraic and satisfy Hironaka’s box condition (to be defined below, see section 3), Lafon in the principal ideal case and Hironaka in general have shown that the remainder of the division is again an algebraic series [Lf, Hi1], cf.÷ also [BCR, Thm.÷ 8.2.9, p.÷ 169]. As a consequence, the reduced standard basis of the ideal is also formed by algebraic series. This fact was used for instance by Hironaka in order to construct idealistic exponents of singularities on étale neighborhoods and to control the behaviour of the local resolution invariant ν∗\nu^{*} under blowup [Hi1, Hi2, chap.÷ III].

The beforementioned box condition is the natural extension to the case of ideals of the notion of xnx_{n}-regularity of a series. It postulates the existence of a specific Rees decomposition – namely one which is generated by monomials in an appropriate coordinate system – of the quotient module of the power series ring factored by the given ideal, cf.÷ [Re] and section 2. Algorithms to determine Rees decompositions have been proposed by Sturmfels-White [SW]. They rely on the construction of (not necessarily reduced) standard bases.

Starting with a system of algebraic generators of an ideal with box condition it is not at all clear how to construct, from the polynomial codes of the generators, the codes of the algebraic series defining the reduced standard basis, or, respectively, the codes of the quotients and the remainder of the division of a given algebraic series by the ideal. This question will be the subject of the article.

We prove that there does exist a finite algorithm which computes the codes of the reduced standard basis, respectively of the quotient and the remainder series of a division, from the codes of the algebraic input series. For the principal ideal case, i.e., the Weierstrass division, such an algorithm has been proposed and proven to work by Alonso-Mora-Raimondo [AMR]. This algorithm is already quite complicated. The general case, i.e., the division of one series by several series, is substantially more intricate and resisted for a long time.

In this paper we will present a complete answer to the problem, describing explicitly how to manipulate the codes of algebraic power series in order to perform the division in general. This, of course, reproves Lafon’s and Hironaka’s existential results on division, but it goes far beyond: It provides a quite precise manual of how to express algebraic operations with algebraic power series in terms of their codes. This is by no means trivial, and the resulting algorithm, when carried out in a concrete example, turns out to have high complexity (we give one explicit computation in the appendix). So for practical purposes the algorithm is of no big use.

But taken from a logical or operational point of view, the algorithm is very interesting. It is built on two simultaneous inductions, both on the number of variables, which resemble the induction which appears in the proof of the Artin approximation theorem [Ar2]. Coordinates in the affine space and generators of the ideals have to be chosen very carefully so as to make the argument work. But once this is done appropriately, the proofs develop quite naturally and are almost straightforward. In this sense, we are not only able to codify algebraic power series – we know and understand how this codification mimics their manipulation in the division process.

Behind the curtain, there resides a finiteness principle which is ubiquituous in algebraic geometry and commutative algebra: The Noether normalization lemma, or, phrased differently, the finiteness of certain morphisms. In our context, this finiteness is first met in the notion of xnx_{n}-regularity of power series in the Weierstrass division, and then also in Hironaka’s box condition and our concept of echelon (which is a Rees decomposition of a prescribed combinatorial type). It is the prerequisite for a subtle induction on the number of variables, but has the drawback that in the induction step one has to consider modules instead of ideals. This aggravates the notation, though modules are the natural context to work with.

The nicest part of our algorithm is what we call virtual division, a trick which has already appeared in various disguises in the literature, e.g.÷ in the work of Artin, Malgrange, Mora, Pfister-Popescu and Alonso-Mora-Raimondo: When dividing formal power series expand them with respect to one variable and write the coefficient series in the remaining variables as new unknown variables. If this is done with the necessary caution, the successive operations in the division of the formal power series can be carried out in terms of these virtual series and will then be finite processes. To make this approach work in reality, a precise understanding of the structure of the division algorithm is mandatory.

To resume and rephrase the above, our division algorithm for the codes of algebraic power series shows that the division is a finite process once you succeed to interpret certain packages of infinitely many data (i.e., coefficient series) as single objects which undergo a uniform transformation under division. The complexity of the algorithm shows that this encryption is by no means obvious. But it does exist and work.

The emphasis of the paper is theoretical – actual computations become quickly unfeasable. We rather provide insight and methods of how to manipulate algebraic power series abstractly within finite algorithms. This may turn out to be useful in other situations where one aims at or needs finiteness assertions: passage to étale neighborhoods, noetherianity, semicontinuity of invariants of complete local rings, recursion theory for generating series, …

Example. Let us briefly explain the method in the special case of the construction of the code of the Weierstrass normal form of an xnx_{n}-regular power series g⁡(x)g(x) of order dd. Assume for simplicity that gg is actually a polynomial, say g⁡(x)=G⁡(x)∈K⁡[x]g(x)=G(x)\in K[x] (capital letters will be reserved throughout for polynomials). Introduce new variables u0,…,ud−1u_{0},\ldots,u_{d-1} and define a polynomial B∈K⁡[xn,u]B\in K[x_{n},u] as B⁡(xn,u)=xnd+∑j=0d−1uj⋅xnjB(x_{n},u)=x_{n}^{d}+\sum_{j=0}^{d-1}u_{j}\cdot x_{n}^{j}. This is our candidate presentation for the Weierstrass normal form of GG. It then suffices to determine (algebraic) series u0​(x′),…,ud−1​(x′)∈K⁡[[x′]]=K⁡[[x1,…,xn−1]]u_{0}(x^{\prime}),\ldots,u_{d-1}(x^{\prime})\in K[[x^{\prime}]]=K[[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n-1}]] such that the series b⁡(x)b(x) obtained from BB by substitution of uju_{j} by uj​(x′)u_{j}(x^{\prime}), say

b⁡(x)=B⁡(xn,u⁡(x′))=xnd+∑j=0d−1uj​(x′)⋅xnjb(x)=B(x_{n},u(x^{\prime}))=x_{n}^{d}+\sum_{j=0}^{d-1}u_{j}(x^{\prime})\cdot x_{n}^{j},

equals the Weierstrass normal form of GG. Instead of constructing the series uj​(x′)u_{j}(x^{\prime}) directly, we shall develop a procedure to determine their code (in the sense described above, see section 6 for details). To do this, observe first that xndx_{n}^{d} is the initial monomial of GG with respect to the lexicographic order <l​e​x<_{lex} on ℕn{{{\tenmsb N}}}^{n} for which (1,0,…,0)>…>(0,…,0,1)(1,0,\ldots,0)>\ldots>(0,\ldots,0,1), i.e., the exponent of xndx_{n}^{d} is the smallest element with respect to <l​e​x<_{lex} of the support of GG (this uses that uj​(0)=0u_{j}(0)=0 since bb has order dd at 00). The usual power series division of the monomial xndx_{n}^{d} by GG with respect to this initial monomial then yields a formal power series remainder r⁡(x)=∑j=0d−1uj​(x′)⋅xnjr(x)=\sum_{j=0}^{d-1}u_{j}(x^{\prime})\cdot x_{n}^{j} such that xnd−r⁡(x)x_{n}^{d}-r(x) is the Weierstrass normal form of GG. This division is in general an infinite process.

The key point now is to view xndx_{n}^{d} alternatively as the leading monomial of the polynomial BB with respect to a suitable monomial order <ω<_{\omega} on ℕ×ℕd{{{\tenmsb N}}}\times{{{\tenmsb N}}}^{d}, i.e., the exponent of xndx_{n}^{d} becomes the largest element with respect to <ω<_{\omega} of the support of BB. Indeed, just take for <ω<_{\omega} an order such that uj<<xnu_{j}<\!\!<x_{n} for j=0,…,d−1j=0,\ldots,d-1. Then uj⋅xnj<xndu_{j}\cdot x_{n}^{j}<x_{n}^{d} for j<dj<d and hence xndx_{n}^{d} will be the largest monomial of GG with respect to <ω<_{\omega}. This now allows us to divide GG by BB polynomially with respect to the leading monomial xndx_{n}^{d}, say

G=Q⋅B+RG=Q\cdot B+R,

with quotient a polynomial QQ in K⁡[x,u]K[x,u] and with remainder a polynomial RR in K⁡[x,u]K[x,u] of the form R=∑j=0d−1Uj​(x′,u)⋅xnjR=\sum_{j=0}^{d-1}U_{j}(x^{\prime},u)\cdot x_{n}^{j} for some polynomial coefficients Uj∈K⁡[x′,u]U_{j}\in K[x^{\prime},u]. If gg were not a polynomial but just an algebraic series, one would have to take for GG the polynomial code of it, see section 13 for the precise procedure. This polynomial division is, of course, a finite process. A rather tedious computation then shows that the jacobian matrix ∂uU\partial_{u}U of the vector U=(U0,…,Ud−1)∈K​[x′,u]dU=(U_{0},\ldots,U_{d-1})\in K[x^{\prime},u]^{d} with respect to the uu-variables is invertible when evaluated at 00. It thus defines, by the implicit function theorem, a unique vector u⁡(x′)=(u0​(x′),…,ud−1​(x′))u(x^{\prime})=(u_{0}(x^{\prime}),\ldots,u_{d-1}(x^{\prime})) of algebraic series uj​(x′)u_{j}(x^{\prime}) such that U⁡(x′,u⁡(x′))=0U(x^{\prime},u(x^{\prime}))=0. This just means that UU is a code for u⁡(x′)u(x^{\prime}). But, by construction, R⁡(x,u⁡(x′))=0R(x,u(x^{\prime}))=0, so that G⁡(x)=Q⁡(x,u⁡(x′))⋅B⁡(x,u⁡(x′))G(x)=Q(x,u(x^{\prime}))\cdot B(x,u(x^{\prime})). By comparison of the initial monomials it follows that Q⁡(x,u⁡(x′))Q(x,u(x^{\prime})) is invertible as a power series, hence b⁡(x)=B⁡(x,u⁡(x′))b(x)=B(x,u(x^{\prime})) is indeed the Weierstrass normal form of GG as required.

This example gives an idea of how the codes of reduced standard bases and of the quotients and the remainder of a division can be constructed. In practice and for the required generality the technicalities become unfortunately much more involved.

At the same time, there remain puzzling mysteries when the involved algebraic series are no longer xnx_{n}-regular (in which case the Weierstrass normal form has to be defined as the reduced standard basis of the ideal). For instance, the polynomial x​y−z⁡(x+y+x2​y2)xy-z(x+y+x^{2}y^{2}) with initial monomial x​yxy has an algebraic series as its normal form, whereas the normal form of x​y−z⁡(x2+y2+x2​y2)xy-z(x^{2}+y^{2}+x^{2}y^{2}) is a transcendent series (over a ground field of characteristic zero; it is a so called Mahler series). Both facts are easy to prove by direct computation. In contrast, the normal form of x​y−z⁡(1+y)​(1+x2​y)xy-z(1+y)(1+x^{2}y), a polynomial which appears in the counting of Gessel walks, is again an algebraic series, but this seems to be very intricate to prove. The algebraicity of the normal form was eventually shown by Bostan-Kauers – a substantial part of their proof relies on heavy computer machinery [BK]. No conceptual systematic proof of the algebraicity seems to be known for this example. However, modifying slightly the input polynomial, taking now x​y−z⁡(1+y)​(1+x​y2)xy-z(1+y)(1+xy^{2}), it is almost immediate to detect the algebraicity using a suitable division.

These examples suggest that there are hidden structural patterns which cause the phenomena to happen and which should explain the occurrence of algebraic or transcendent normal forms. Little seems to be known in this respect. For instance, the classification of the generating functions of lattice walks in the first quadrant, studied among others by Bousquet-Mélou, Mishna and Petkovšek, does not seem to reveal a systematic background [BM, BP2, Mi].

Organization of the paper. After some preliminary recalls on the formal power series and polynomial division covering sections 2 to 5, we introduce and study in sections 6 to 8 codes of algebraic series and of the ideals generated by them. These are polynomial data which completely determine the series and ideals they encode. For later purposes the codification is carried out from the beginning for vectors of algebraic series and the modules they generate.

Section 9 describes how to compute the codes of standard bases of ideals and modules from a given (arbitrary) generator system (Theorem 9.1). This is straightforward, and based on Lazard’s homogenization method, respectively Mora’s tangent cone algorithm. Both were refined and extended by Gräbe and Greuel-Pfister. Our two main results (sections 10 and 11) concern the construction – in terms of the defining codes – of reduced standard bases of modules of algebraic power series vectors (Theorem 10.1), and of the quotients and the remainder of an algebraic power series division (Theorem 11.1).

The proofs of these two theorems are mutually interwoven (sections 12 to 15). First, the construction of the reduced standard basis is performed in the xnx_{n}-regular case (i.e., in the case where the initial module of the given module of algebraic power series vectors is generated by monomial vectors depending only on the last variable xnx_{n}). This is by far the most complicated step. It clearly shows how important it is to codify the series in a very systematic manner. Otherwise it would be hopeless to prove that the resulting polynomial vectors represent again codes (i.e., satisfy the assumption of the implicit function theorem). In the case of principal ideals, the proof provides the code of the Weierstrass normal form of the given series, cf.÷ [AMR].

The preceding construction of the codes of the reduced standard basis in the xnx_{n}-regular case is then used to establish the division of algebraic series on the level of codes in the xnx_{n}-regular case. This is not too difficult. It relies on the effectivity of the division algorithm in localizations of polynomial rings, proven by Lazard, Mora, Gräbe and Greuel-Pfister.

Once the two theorems are established in the xnx_{n}-regular case, the general case is carried out by induction on the number of variables. It is here that Hironaka’s box condition comes into play. One key feature is its persistence under taking hyperplane sections (in a well defined sense), and this is used to know that the associated modules in n−1n-1 variables satisfy again the box condition. So induction applies to prove both theorems simultaneously.

In the last section, we illustrate the instances and the complexity of the two algorithms in the computation of a concrete example.

2. Monomial modules

The letters nn, pp, rr, ss are reserved for fixed integers in ℕ{{{\tenmsb N}}}. The letters ii, kk and ℓ\ell will generally vary in the ranges 1≤i≤p1\leq i\leq p, 1≤k≤r1\leq k\leq r and 1≤ℓ≤s1\leq\ell\leq s.

We denote by K⁡[x1,…,xn]=K⁡[x]K[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}]=K[x] and K⁡[[x1,…,xn]]=K⁡[[x]]K[[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}]]=K[[x]] the polynomial, respectively formal power series ring in nn variables x=(x1,…,xn)x=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}) over a field KK. Elements of K​[x]sK[x]^{s} and K​[[x]]sK[[x]]^{s} will be called polynomial respectively formal power series vectors. Capital letters will be reserved for polynomials, lower case letters for power series. We set x′=(x1,…,xn−1)x^{\prime}=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n-1}) and denote by y=(y1,…,yp)y=(y_{1},\ldots,y_{p}) additional variables.

Vectors g∈K​[[x]]sg\in K[[x]]^{s} will be expanded into g=∑α​ℓcα​ℓ​xα​eℓg=\sum_{\alpha\ell}c_{\alpha\ell}x^{\alpha}e_{\ell} with cα​ℓ∈Kc_{\alpha\ell}\in K and eℓ=(0,…,0,1,0,…,0)e_{\ell}=(0,\ldots,0,1,0,\ldots,0) the canonical KK-basis of KsK^{s}. The vectors xα​eℓx^{\alpha}e_{\ell} are called monomial vectors. Note that all their entries but one are zero: a vector all whose entries are monomials will not be considered here as a monomial vector. The support of gg is the set supp⁡(g)={(α,ℓ)∈ℕn×{1,…,s},cα​ℓ≠0}{\rm supp}(g)=\{(\alpha,\ell)\in{{{\tenmsb N}}}^{n}\times\{1,\ldots,s\},\,c_{\alpha\ell}\neq 0\}. We sometimes abbreviate pairs (α,ℓ)(\alpha,\ell) by α​ℓ\alpha\ell.

Brackets ⟨g1,…,gr⟩\langle g_{1},\ldots,g_{r}\rangle denote submodules of K​[[x]]sK[[x]]^{s} generated by power series vectors g1,…,gr∈K​[[x]]sg_{1},\ldots,g_{r}\in K[[x]]^{s}. We abbreviate this by ⟨gk⟩\langle g_{k}\rangle if the range of kk is clear from the context.

A monomial submodule of K​[[x]]sK[[x]]^{s} is a submodule MM of K​[[x]]sK[[x]]^{s} generated by monomial vectors. It is a cartesian product M=Πℓ=1s​MℓM=\Pi_{\ell=1}^{s}M_{\ell} of monomial ideals MℓM_{\ell} in K⁡[[x]]K[[x]]. The elements of MM are the power series vectors with support in Σ={(α,ℓ)∈ℕn×{1,…,s},xα​eℓ∈M}\Sigma=\{(\alpha,\ell)\in{{{\tenmsb N}}}^{n}\times\{1,\ldots,s\},\,x^{\alpha}e_{\ell}\in M\}. The canonical direct monomial complement of a monomial submodule MM of K​[[x]]sK[[x]]^{s} is the subvectorspace co⁡(M){\rm co}(M) of K​[[x]]sK[[x]]^{s} of power series vectors with support in Σ′=(ℕn×{1,…,s})∖Σ\Sigma^{\prime}=({{{\tenmsb N}}}^{n}\times\{1,\ldots,s\})\setminus\Sigma. This provides the direct sum decomposition of KK-vectorspaces M⊕co⁡(M)=K​[[x]]sM\oplus{\rm co}(M)=K[[x]]^{s}.

We say that a monomial submodule MM of K​[[x]]sK[[x]]^{s} is xnx_{n}-regular if it is generated by monomial vectors in K​[[xn]]sK[[x_{n}]]^{s}, say M=⟨M∩K​[[xn]]s⟩M=\langle M\cap K[[x_{n}]]^{s}\rangle. We shall then always assume for simplicity – applying if necessary a permutation of the components of K​[[x]]sK[[x]]^{s} – that MM is generated by vectors of the form xndk⋅ekx_{n}^{d_{k}}\cdot e_{k} with dk≥0d_{k}\geq 0 and 1≤k≤r1\leq k\leq r for some r≤sr\leq s. In this case the complement co⁡(M){\rm co}(M) is a cartesian product

co(M)=∏k=1r(⊕j=0dk−1K[[x′]]⋅xnj)×K[[x]]s−r{\rm co}(M)=\prod_{k=1}^{r}(\oplus_{j=0}^{d_{k}-1}K[[x^{\prime}]]\cdot x_{n}^{j})\times K[[x]]^{s-r}

of a finitely generated free K⁡[[x′]]K[[x^{\prime}]]-module with a finitely generated free K⁡[[x]]K[[x]]-module. We say that MM satisfies Hironaka’s box condition if co⁡(M){\rm co}(M) can be written as a cartesian product of direct sums of finite free monomial K⁡[[x1,…,xj]]K[[x_{1},\ldots,x_{j}]]-modules

co(M)=∏ℓ=1s⊕j=0n⊕γ∈Γℓ​jK[[x1,…,xj]]⋅xγ{\rm co}(M)=\prod_{\ell=1}^{s}\,\oplus_{j=0}^{n}\,\oplus_{\gamma\in\Gamma_{\ell j}}K[[x_{1},\ldots,x_{j}]]\cdot x^{\gamma}

with finite sets Γℓ​j⊂ℕn\Gamma_{\ell j}\subset{{{\tenmsb N}}}^{n}. Being xnx_{n}-regular is a special case of the box condition. For cyclic submodules of K​[[x]]sK[[x]]^{s}, both notions coincide. They obviously depend on the numbering of the variables x1,…,xnx_{1},\ldots,x_{n}. Notice that for s=1s=1 and 0≠M⊊K⁡[[x]]0\neq M\mathchar 14632\relax K[[x]] a non trivial ideal, the indices of the boxes FjF_{j} run from 11 to n−1n-1. Also notice that the box condition for a monomial submodule M⊂K​[[x]]sM\subset K[[x]]^{s} is equivalent to the box condition for each of the factors of MM (which are monomial ideals in K⁡[[x]]K[[x]]).

W.÷ Seiler informed us that in the case of ideals the box condition is equivalent to his notion of δ\delta-regular coordinates [Se3]. We say that a monomial submodule MM of K​[[x]]sK[[x]]^{s} is an echelon if it can be written as

M=∏ℓ=1s⊕j=0n⊕δ∈Δℓ​jK[[x1,…,xj]]⋅xδM=\prod_{\ell=1}^{s}\,\oplus_{j=0}^{n}\,\oplus_{\delta\in\Delta_{\ell j}}K[[x_{1},\ldots,x_{j}]]\cdot x^{\delta}

with finite sets Δℓ​j⊂ℕn\Delta_{\ell j}\subset{{{\tenmsb N}}}^{n}. This can be rewritten as

M=⊕ℓ=1s⊕δ∈ΔℓK[[x1,…,xnδ]]⋅xδ⋅eℓM=\oplus_{\ell=1}^{s}\,\,\oplus_{\delta\in\Delta_{\ell}}K[[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n_{\delta}}]]\cdot x^{\delta}\cdot e_{\ell}

where Δℓ=⋃jΔℓ​j\Delta_{\ell}=\bigcup_{j}\Delta_{\ell j} and where, for each δ\delta, the index nδn_{\delta} takes a value between 00 and nn. This notion is a special case of a Rees decomposition of MM [Re]. We call the collection of monomial vectors xδ⋅eℓx^{\delta}\cdot e_{\ell} with δ∈Δℓ\delta\in\Delta_{\ell} and 1≤ℓ≤s1\leq\ell\leq s a Janet basis of the echelon MM with scopes nδn_{\delta} (also known as levels or classes). Our definition differs slightly from Janet’s original definition in the sense that we only allow nested groups of variables in the coefficients [Ja1, Ja2], cf.÷ also [Ri]. We refer to the related notions of Pommaret bases and involutive bases [GB, Se1, Se2], and the more general concepts of Rees and Stanley decompositions of rings [Re, SW, Am, BG].

For the following result, see also Janet [Ja1, Ja2] and Seiler [Se2].

Theorem 2.1. Monomial submodules of K​[[x]]sK[[x]]^{s} satisfying Hironaka’s box conditon are echelons.

Proof. Let MM be such a module, and let Mn=⟨M∩K​[[xn]]s⟩M_{n}=\langle M\cap K[[x_{n}]]^{s}\rangle be the submodule of K​[[x]]sK[[x]]^{s} generated by the xnx_{n}-pure monomial vectors of MM. By definition, MnM_{n} is xnx_{n}-regular. Let xndk⋅ekx_{n}^{d_{k}}\cdot e_{k} with 1≤k≤r1\leq k\leq r be a minimal generator system of MnM_{n} (after possibly permuting the components of K​[[x]]sK[[x]]^{s}). Then Mn=⊕k=1rK[[x]]⋅xndk⋅ekM_{n}=\oplus_{k=1}^{r}K[[x]]\cdot x_{n}^{d_{k}}\cdot e_{k}, which shows that the monomial vectors xndk⋅ekx_{n}^{d_{k}}\cdot e_{k} form a Janet basis of MnM_{n} with scopes nk=nn_{k}=n. The direct sum decomposition

K[[x]]s=Mn⊕(⊕m=1r⊕j=0dm−1K[[x′]]⋅xnj⋅em)⊕⊕m=r+1sK[[x]]⋅emK[[x]]^{s}=M_{n}\oplus(\oplus_{m=1}^{r}\,\oplus_{j=0}^{d_{m}-1}K[[x^{\prime}]]\cdot x_{n}^{j}\cdot e_{m})\,\,\oplus\,\,\oplus_{m=r+1}^{s}\,K[[x]]\cdot e_{m}

yields a decomposition M=Mn⊕M′M=M_{n}\oplus M^{\prime} where M′M^{\prime} is now a K⁡[[x′]]K[[x^{\prime}]]-submodule of the finitely generated free K⁡[[x′]]K[[x^{\prime}]]-module ⊕m=1r⊕j=0dm−1K[[x′]]⋅xnj⋅em\oplus_{m=1}^{r}\,\oplus_{j=0}^{d_{m}-1}K[[x^{\prime}]]\cdot x_{n}^{j}\cdot e_{m}. We use here that, because of the box condition, MM has zero intersection with ⊕m=r+1sK[[x]]⋅em\oplus_{m=r+1}^{s}\,K[[x]]\cdot e_{m}.

It is checked that the box condition persists under the above decomposition, i.e., that M′M^{\prime} satisfies it again. By induction on the number of variables, M′M^{\prime} is an echelon. Its Janet basis has scopes ≤n−1\leq n-1. From M=Mn⊕M′M=M_{n}\oplus M^{\prime} now follows that also MM is an echelon.

Example. The assertion of the theorem does not hold for arbitrary modules as was pointed out by W.÷ Seiler. Take the ideal II of K⁡[x,y,z]K[x,y,z] generated by the three monomials x​yxy, x​zxz and y​zyz. It is easy to see that it does not satisfy the box condition. And it is not an echelon, since, for instance, among the monomials of II which are not multiples of x​yxy one has monomials xd​zx^{d}z and yd​zy^{d}z of arbitrary degree dd in xx and yy. As the situation is symmetric with respect to any permutation of the variables, II does not admit the required decomposition of an echelon.

3. Monomial orders and initial modules

Division theorems are based on ordering the summands cα​ℓ​xα​eℓc_{\alpha\ell}x^{\alpha}e_{\ell} of the expansion of a power series vector g=∑α​ℓcα​ℓ​xα​eℓg=\sum_{\alpha\ell}c_{\alpha\ell}x^{\alpha}e_{\ell} according to the indices (α,ℓ)∈ℕn×{1,…,s}(\alpha,\ell)\in{{{\tenmsb N}}}^{n}\times\{1,\ldots,s\} with non-zero coefficients cα​ℓc_{\alpha\ell}: A monomial order on ℕn×{1,…,s}{{{\tenmsb N}}}^{n}\times\{1,\ldots,s\} is a total order <η<_{\eta} on ℕn×{1,…,s}{{{\tenmsb N}}}^{n}\times\{1,\ldots,s\} which is compatible with the semi-group structure of ℕn{{{\tenmsb N}}}^{n}, having 00 as its smallest element, and which is noetherian. This means that if (α,ℓ)<η(β,m)(\alpha,\ell)<_{\eta}(\beta,m) then (α+γ,ℓ)<η(β+γ,m)(\alpha+\gamma,\ell)<_{\eta}(\beta+\gamma,m) for any γ∈ℕn\gamma\in{{{\tenmsb N}}}^{n}, and, secondly, that any decreasing sequence becomes stationary. The order is degree compatible if |α|<|β||\alpha|<|\beta| implies (α,ℓ)<η(β,m)(\alpha,\ell)<_{\eta}(\beta,m), where |α||\alpha| denotes the sum of the components of α\alpha. An extension of <η<_{\eta} is a monomial order <ε<_{\varepsilon} on ℕn+p×{1,…,s}{{{\tenmsb N}}}^{n+p}\times\{1,\ldots,s\} whose restrictions to ℕn×{δ}×{1,…,s}{{{\tenmsb N}}}^{n}\times\{\delta\}\times\{1,\ldots,s\} coincide for all δ∈ℕp\delta\in{{{\tenmsb N}}}^{p} with the order induced by <η<_{\eta} on ℕn×{δ}×{1,…,s}{{{\tenmsb N}}}^{n}\times\{\delta\}\times\{1,\ldots,s\}. We will always identify monomial orders on ℕn×{1,…,s}{{{\tenmsb N}}}^{n}\times\{1,\ldots,s\} with the induded ordering of the monomial vectors in K​[[x]]sK[[x]]^{s}.

The initial monomial vector in⁡(g){\rm in}(g) of g=∑cα​ℓ​xα​eℓ∈K​[[x]]sg=\sum c_{\alpha\ell}x^{\alpha}e_{\ell}\in K[[x]]^{s} with respect to <η<_{\eta} is the vector xα⋅eℓx^{\alpha}\cdot e_{\ell} of the expansion of gg for which (α,ℓ)(\alpha,\ell) is minimal with respect to <η<_{\eta}. We shall assume that xα⋅eℓx^{\alpha}\cdot e_{\ell} has coefficient 11 in the expansion of gg. We then write g=xα⋅eℓ−g¯g=x^{\alpha}\cdot e_{\ell}-\overline{g} and call g¯\overline{g} the tail of gg.

For a submodule II of K​[[x]]sK[[x]]^{s}, the initial module of II with respect to <η<_{\eta} is the monomial submodule in⁡(I){\rm in}(I) of K​[[x]]sK[[x]]^{s} generated by all initial monomial vectors of elements of II. This is a monomial submodule which depends on the choice of <η<_{\eta}. We denote by co⁡(I){\rm co}(I) the canonical direct monomial complement of in⁡(I){\rm in}(I) in K​[[x]]sK[[x]]^{s}. Elements g1,…,grg_{1},\ldots,g_{r} of K​[[x]]sK[[x]]^{s} form a standard basis w.r.t.÷ <η<_{\eta} if their initial monomial vectors generate the initial module in⁡(I){\rm in}(I) of the module II generated by g1,…,grg_{1},\ldots,g_{r}. They are a reduced standard basis if the tails g¯k\overline{g}_{k} belong to co⁡(I){\rm co}(I). We do not require that a reduced standard basis is minimal.

We say that a submodule II of K​[[x]]sK[[x]]^{s} is xnx_{n}-regular, respectively satisfies Hironaka’s box condition, or is an echelon with respect to the monomial order <η<_{\eta} on ℕn×{1,…,s}{{{\tenmsb N}}}^{n}\times\{1,\ldots,s\}, if its initial module in⁡(I){\rm in}(I) is xnx_{n}-regular, respectively satisfies the box condition, or is an echelon. A Janet basis of a submodule II of K​[[x]]sK[[x]]^{s} which is an echelon w.r.t.÷ <η<_{\eta} is a generator system g1,…,grg_{1},\ldots,g_{r} of II whose initial monomial vectors in⁡(gk){\rm in}(g_{k}) form a Janet basis of in⁡(I){\rm in}(I).

For a polynomial vector G∈K​[x]sG\in K[x]^{s}, define the leading monomial vector lm⁡(G){\rm lm}(G) as the monomial vector xα​eℓx^{\alpha}e_{\ell} of the expansion of GG which is maximal with respect to the chosen monomial order. Similarly as for initial modules, one obtains now the leading module lm⁡(I){\rm lm}(I) of a submodule II of K​[x]sK[x]^{s}.

4. Division of formal power series and polynomials

We recall the division theorem for modules of formal power series of Grauert, Hironaka and Galligo [AHV, Gra, Hi1, Ga, HM]. For extensions of this result to more general settings see [Am, BG, GB, Se2].

Theorem 4.1. Let II be a submodule of K​[[x]]sK[[x]]^{s} with initial module in⁡(I){\rm in}(I) with respect to a monomial order <η<_{\eta} on ℕn×{1,…,s}{{{\tenmsb N}}}^{n}\times\{1,\ldots,s\}. Let co⁡(I){\rm co}(I) be the canonical direct monomial complement of in⁡(I){\rm in}(I) in K​[[x]]sK[[x]]^{s}. Then I⊕co⁡(I)=K​[[x]]sI\oplus{\rm co}(I)=K[[x]]^{s}.

Sketch of proof. The sum I⊕co⁡(I)I\oplus{\rm co}(I) is direct by definition of co⁡(I){\rm co}(I). To see that it equals K​[[x]]sK[[x]]^{s}, choose a standard basis g1,…,grg_{1},\ldots,g_{r} of II. It suffices to show that the linear map u:K​[[x]]r×co⁡(I)→K​[[x]]s,(a1,…,ar,b)→∑ak​gk+bu:K[[x]]^{r}\times{\rm co}(I)\rightarrow K[[x]]^{s},\,(a_{1},\ldots,a_{r},b)\rightarrow\sum a_{k}g_{k}+b is surjective. By definition of standard bases, the map v:K​[[x]]r×co⁡(I)→K​[[x]]s,(a1,…,ar,b)→∑ak⋅in⁡(gk)+bv:K[[x]]^{r}\times{\rm co}(I)\rightarrow K[[x]]^{s},\,(a_{1},\ldots,a_{r},b)\rightarrow\sum a_{k}\cdot{\rm in}(g_{k})+b is surjective. Writing u=v+wu=v+w, the assertion follows by restricting vv to a direct complement LL of its kernel and by showing that u|L=v|L+w|Lu_{|L}=v_{|L}+w_{|L} is an isomorphism with inverse the geometric series (v|L)−1∑j=0∞((v|L)−1w|L)j(v_{|L})^{-1}\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}((v_{|L})^{-1}w_{|L})^{j}. This series then induces the required linear map K​[[x]]s→LK[[x]]^{s}\rightarrow L inverse to u|Lu_{|L}, see [HM, Thm.÷ 5.1] for details.

The division theorem can be formulated more explicitly as follows: If g1,…,grg_{1},\ldots,g_{r} generate II, each vector f∈K​[[x]]sf\in K[[x]]^{s} has a decomposition f=∑kak​gk+hf=\sum_{k}a_{k}g_{k}+h with unique h∈co⁡(I)h\in{\rm co}(I). The power series expansions of the quotients aka_{k} and the remainder hh can be computed up to any given degree by a finite algorithm (take the expansion of the geometric series above up to the respective degree). The requirement that hh belongs to co⁡(I){\rm co}(I) makes the remainder independent of the choice of g1,…,grg_{1},\ldots,g_{r} (but it depends on the monomial order <η<_{\eta}). If g1,…,grg_{1},\ldots,g_{r} form a standard basis, the quotients aka_{k} can be made unique by imposing suitable support conditions on them [Ga]. A reduced standard basis of II is given as xα⋅eℓ−hα​ℓx^{\alpha}\cdot e_{\ell}-h_{\alpha\ell} with (α,ℓ)(\alpha,\ell) varying in some finite subset V⊂ℕn×{1,…,s}V\subset{{{\tenmsb N}}}^{n}\times\{1,\ldots,s\}, where the vectors xα⋅eℓx^{\alpha}\cdot e_{\ell} are generators of in⁡(I){\rm in}(I) and the vectors hα​ℓh_{\alpha\ell} denote the remainder of the division of xα⋅eℓx^{\alpha}\cdot e_{\ell} by II.

For modules which are echelons one can formulate a more precise statement:

Theorem 4.2. Let II be a submodule of K​[[x]]sK[[x]]^{s} with initial module in⁡(I){\rm in}(I) w.r.t.÷ a monomial order <η<_{\eta} on ℕn×{1,…,s}{{{\tenmsb N}}}^{n}\times\{1,\ldots,s\}. Assume that II is an echelon, and let xα⋅eℓx^{\alpha}\cdot e_{\ell} be a Janet basis of in⁡(I){\rm in}(I) with scopes nα​ℓn_{\alpha\ell}, (α,ℓ)(\alpha,\ell) varying in some finite set V⊂ℕn×{1,…,s}V\subset{{{\tenmsb N}}}^{n}\times\{1,\ldots,s\}. Choose any elements gα​ℓg_{\alpha\ell} of II with initial monomial vectors xα⋅eℓx^{\alpha}\cdot e_{\ell}. Then

I⊕co(I)=⊕α​ℓ∈VK[[x1,…,xnα​ℓ]]⋅gα​ℓ⊕co(I)=K[[x]]sI\oplus{\rm co}(I)=\oplus_{\alpha\ell\in V}\ K[[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n_{\alpha\ell}}]]\cdot g_{\alpha\ell}\oplus{\rm co}(I)=K[[x]]^{s}.

Proof. First notice that in(I)=⊕α​ℓ∈VK[[x1,…,xnα​ℓ]]⋅xα⋅eℓ{\rm in}(I)=\oplus_{\alpha\ell\in V}\ K[[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n_{\alpha\ell}}]]\cdot x^{\alpha}\cdot e_{\ell} by definition of echelons. This allows us to modify the map uu from the proof of the division theorem by restricting it to the KK-subspace

⊕α​ℓ∈VK[[x1,…,xnα​ℓ]]⋅xα⋅eℓ×co(I)\oplus_{\alpha\ell\in V}\ K[[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n_{\alpha\ell}}]]\cdot x^{\alpha}\cdot e_{\ell}\times{\rm co}(I).

The map vv is then by construction an isomorphism, and the same reasoning as before shows that this holds also for uu. This proves the claim.

In the polynomial case, the division admits an analogous formulation. The same proof as above applies, because the evaluation of the geometric series (v|L)−1∑j=0∞((v|L)−1w|L)j(v_{|L})^{-1}\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}((v_{|L})^{-1}w_{|L})^{j} on a polynomial vector (a1,…,ar,b)∈K​[x]r×co⁡(I)(a_{1},\ldots,a_{r},b)\in K[x]^{r}\times{\rm co}(I) terminates at sufficiently large jj.

Theorem 4.3. Let II be a submodule of K​[x]sK[x]^{s} with leading module lm⁡(I){\rm lm}(I) with respect to a monomial order <η<_{\eta} on ℕn×{1,…,s}{{{\tenmsb N}}}^{n}\times\{1,\ldots,s\}. Let co⁡(I){\rm co}(I) be the canonical direct monomial complement of lm⁡(I){\rm lm}(I) in K​[x]sK[x]^{s}. Then I⊕co⁡(I)=K​[x]sI\oplus{\rm co}(I)=K[x]^{s}.

Again, there is a more precise version in case the leading module lm⁡(I){\rm lm}(I) is an echelon.

Theorem 4.4. Let II be a submodule of K​[x]sK[x]^{s} with leading monomial module lm⁡(I){\rm lm}(I) with respect to a monomial order <η<_{\eta} on ℕn×{1,…,s}{{{\tenmsb N}}}^{n}\times\{1,\ldots,s\}. Assume that lm⁡(I){\rm lm}(I) is an echelon. Let GkG_{k} be a polynomial Janet basis of II with leading monomial vectors lm⁡(Gk){\rm lm}(G_{k}) of scope nkn_{k}. Then any F∈K​[x]sF\in K[x]^{s} admits a unique division

F=∑kAk​Gk+CF=\sum_{k}A_{k}G_{k}+C

with Ak∈K⁡[x1,…,xnk]A_{k}\in K[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n_{k}}] and C∈co⁡(I)C\in{\rm co}(I). The decomposition can be obtained from the polynomial vectors FF and GkG_{k} by a finite algorithm.

5. Algebraic power series

Algebraic power series are formal power series h⁡(x)=∑α∈ℕncα​xαh(x)=\sum_{\alpha\in{{{\sevenmsb N}}}^{n}}c_{\alpha}x^{\alpha} in several variables x=(x1,…,xn)x=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}) with coefficients in a field KK which satisfy an algebraic relation of the form

P⁡(x,h⁡(x))=pd​hd+pd−1​hd−1+…+p1​h+p0=0P(x,h(x))=p_{d}h^{d}+p_{d-1}h^{d-1}+\ldots+p_{1}h+p_{0}=0,

where the coefficients pi=pi​(x)p_{i}=p_{i}(x) are polynomials. We refer to [Ar2, BCR, BrK, KPR, Lf, Na1, Na2, Ra, Ru, Wi] for the respective background. An algebraic power series vector is a vector in K​[[x]]sK[[x]]^{s} whose components are algebraic series.

Typical algebraic series are rational functions as x⋅(1+x)−1x\cdot(1+x)^{-1}, roots of polynomials as 1+x2​y\sqrt{1+x^{2}y}, inverses f−1f^{-1} of polynomial mappings f:Kn→Knf:K^{n}\rightarrow K^{n} satisfying at a point pp the assumption of the Inverse Function Theorem as f⁡(x,y)=(x+x3,y−x​y2)f(x,y)=(x+x^{3},y-xy^{2}) at 00, or solutions y⁡(x)y(x) of polynomial equations f⁡(x,y)=0f(x,y)=0 satisfying at a point pp the assumption of the implicit function theorem with respect to the variables yy as f⁡(x,y)=y+x​y+x3​y2f(x,y)=y+xy+x^{3}y^{2} at 00.

The ring of algebraic series in nn variables is thus the algebraic closure of the polynomial ring K⁡[x1,…,xn]K[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}] inside the formal power series ring K⁡[[x1,…,xn]]K[[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}]]. It can equivalently be interpreted as the henselization of the polynomial ring at 00.

Note that the minimal polynomial of an algebraic series hh determines hh only up to conjugacy: there may be other power series solutions to the equation, the conjugates of hh, and hh can be distinguished from these for instance by a sufficiently high truncation of its Taylor expansion. The simplest example thereof is the equation y2−2​y+x=0y^{2}-2y+x=0 with algebraic solutions h±=1±1−xh_{\pm}=1\pm\sqrt{1-x}.

Lafon proved in 1965 that the Weierstrass division preserves the algebraicity of the involved series [Lf], see also [BCR]. This was reproven in 2000 by Bousquet-Mélou and Petkovšek working with the recursions defining the coefficients of the series [BP1]. The result of Lafon was extended by Hironaka in 1977 to the division by ideals with several generators satisfying the box condition [Hi1]. We formulate here the division directly for modules.

Theorem 5.1. Let II be a submodule of K​[[x]]sK[[x]]^{s} generated by algebraic power series vectors. Assume that II satisfies Hironaka’s box condition with respect to a monomial order <η<_{\eta} on ℕn×{1,…,s}{{{\tenmsb N}}}^{n}\times\{1,\ldots,s\}. For any algebraic power series vector f∈K​[[x]]sf\in K[[x]]^{s} the remainder cc of the formal power series division of ff by II with respect to <η<_{\eta} is an algebraic power series vector.

The theorem implies in particular that any submodule of K​[[x]]sK[[x]]^{s} with box condition which is generated by algebraic power series vectors admits a reduced standard basis consisting of algebraic power series vectors. Without box condition the remainder of the division need not be algebraic. In [Hi1, p.÷ 75], Hironaka cites the following example of Gabber and Kashiwara, which was rediscovered by Bousquet-Mélou and Petkovs̆ek in combinatorics when counting lattice paths [BP1, BP2].

Example 5.2. Divide x​yxy by g=(x−y2)​(y−x2)=x​y−x3−y3+x2​y2g=(x-y^{2})(y-x^{2})=xy-x^{3}-y^{3}+x^{2}y^{2} as formal power series with respect to the initial monomial x​yxy. The remainder of the division lies in co⁡(x​y)=K⁡[[x]]+K⁡[[y]]{\rm co}(xy)=K[[x]]+K[[y]] and equals the lacunary series b=∑k≥0x3⋅2k+∑k≥0y3⋅2kb=\sum_{k\geq 0}x^{3\cdot 2^{k}}+\sum_{k\geq 0}y^{3\cdot 2^{k}} which is transcendent . Alternatively, we may write x​y=a⋅g+r⁡(x)+s⁡(y)xy=a\cdot g+r(x)+s(y) with series a∈K⁡[[x,y]]a\in K[[x,y]], r∈K⁡[[x]]r\in K[[x]], s∈K⁡[[y]]s\in K[[y]]. The symmetry between xx and yy in this expression yields r⁡(x)=s⁡(x)r(x)=s(x). Substituting yy by x2x^{2} produces x3=a⋅0+r⁡(x)+r⁡(x2)x^{3}=a\cdot 0+r(x)+r(x^{2}) which also gives the expansion of rr.

6. Codes of algebraic power series

In this section we introduce the necessary terminology for working effectively with algebraic power series. The variables x=(x1,…,xn)x=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}) and y=(y1,…,yp)y=(y_{1},\ldots,y_{p}) are fixed throughout.

A mother code (over xx and yy) is a polynomial row vector H=(H1,…,Hp)∈K​[x,y]pH=(H_{1},\ldots,H_{p})\in K[x,y]^{p} with H⁡(0,0)=0H(0,0)=0 whose Jacobian matrix Dy​HD_{y}H with respect to yy is invertible at 00,

Dy​H​(0,0)∈Glp​(K)D_{y}H(0,0)\in{\rm Gl}_{p}(K).

The invertibility of Dy​H​(0,0)D_{y}H(0,0) can be rephrased by saying that for any degree compatible monomial order on ℕp{{{\tenmsb N}}}^{p} the initial ideal of the ideal ⟨H1​(0,y),…,Hp​(0,y)⟩\langle H_{1}(0,y),\ldots,H_{p}(0,y)\rangle of K⁡[[y]]K[[y]] is generated by y1,…,ypy_{1},\ldots,y_{p}. There then exists a linear coordinate change in the yiy_{i}’s so that the initial monomials in​(Hi​(0,y)){\rm in}(H_{i}(0,y)) of Hi​(0,y)H_{i}(0,y) equal yiy_{i}. For any degree compatible monomial order on ℕn+p{{{\tenmsb N}}}^{n+p} so that yi<xjy_{i}<x_{j} for all ii and jj it then follows that the initial monomials in⁡(Hi){\rm in}(H_{i}) of HiH_{i} equal yiy_{i}. Instead of changing the yiy_{i}’s one could also change HH by multiplying it from the right with a suitable matrix in Glp​(K){\rm Gl}_{p}(K) making Dy​H​(0,0)D_{y}H(0,0) unipotent upper triangular. In the sequel we shall always assume that in⁡(Hi)=yi{\rm in}(H_{i})=y_{i} with respect to the chosen monomial order on ℕn+p{{{\tenmsb N}}}^{n+p}.

The baby series vector of a mother code H∈K​[x,y]pH\in K[x,y]^{p} is the formal power series vector h=(h1,…,hp)∈K​[[x]]ph=(h_{1},\ldots,h_{p})\in K[[x]]^{p} vanishing at 00 which is the unique solution of H⁡(x,h⁡(x))=0H(x,h(x))=0. The existence and uniqueness of hh are ensured by the implicit function theorem for formal power series. The components hih_{i} of the baby series vector hh are algebraic series. This can be seen by the algebraic implicit function theorem [KPR, p.÷ 91], or Artin’s Approximation Theorem [Ar2], or by the following argument: Consider the system H⁡(x,y)=0H(x,y)=0 as equations for the last variable ypy_{p}. After a renumeration of the components of HH, the last derivative ∂ypHp​(0,0)\partial_{y_{p}}H_{p}(0,0) does not vanish. There then exists a unique solution hp​(x,y1,…,yp−1)h_{p}(x,y_{1},\ldots,y_{p-1}) of Hp​(x,y1,…,yp−1,yp)=0H_{p}(x,y_{1},\ldots,y_{p-1},y_{p})=0 vanishing at 00, and hph_{p} is algebraic over K⁡[x,y1,…,yp−1]K[x,y_{1},\ldots,y_{p-1}]. By induction on nn and the transitivity of algebraicity we conclude that h=(h1,…,hp)h=(h_{1},\ldots,h_{p}) is algebraic.

An algebraic power series vector h=(h1,…,hp)∈K​[[x]]ph=(h_{1},\ldots,h_{p})\in K[[x]]^{p} is a baby series vector if it admits a mother code H∈K​[x,y]pH\in K[x,y]^{p} defining it.

A father code is a vector G=(G1,…,Gr)G=(G_{1},\ldots,G_{r}) of polynomial vectors Gi∈K​[x,y]sG_{i}\in K[x,y]^{s} (there are no further conditions on the GiG_{i}). We consider GG as a row vector with entries the column vectors GiG_{i}, say as a matrix in K​[x,y]s×rK[x,y]^{s\times r}.

A family code is a pair (H,G)(H,G) where H∈K​[x,y]pH\in K[x,y]^{p} is a mother code and G∈K​[x,y]s×rG\in K[x,y]^{s\times r} a father code, both carrying on the same sets of variables. We say that algebraic power series vectors g1,…,gr∈K​[[x]]sg_{1},\ldots,g_{r}\in K[[x]]^{s} have family code (H,G)∈K​[x,y]p×K​[x,y]s×r(H,G)\in K[x,y]^{p}\times K[x,y]^{s\times r} if

gk=Gk​(x,h⁡(x))g_{k}=G_{k}(x,h(x))

for 1≤k≤r1\leq k\leq r, where h∈K​[[x]]ph\in K[[x]]^{p} is the baby series vector of the mother code HH. The vectors gkg_{k} hence belong to K​[x,h]s⊂K​[[x]]sK[x,h]^{s}\subset K[[x]]^{s}. We call hh the baby series vector underlying g1,…,grg_{1},\ldots,g_{r}, or, the other way round, g1,…,grg_{1},\ldots,g_{r} the algebraic power series vectors produced from hh by the father code GG.

Example 6.1. Take g1=z3+z2​hg_{1}=z^{3}+z^{2}h, g2=x​z2+x​z​hg_{2}=xz^{2}+xzh with baby series h=1−1−x2h=1-\sqrt{1-x^{2}}, mother code H=2​y−y2−x2H=2y-y^{2}-x^{2} and father code G1=z3+z2​yG_{1}=z^{3}+z^{2}y, G2=x​z2+x​z​yG_{2}=xz^{2}+xzy. Notice that the second series solution 1+1−x21+\sqrt{1-x^{2}} of H=0H=0 has non-zero constant term and is therefore not considered as a baby series of HH.

Example 6.2. Let HH be the vector (H1,H2)(H_{1},H_{2}) with H1=y12−2​y1−y2−x2H_{1}=y_{1}^{2}-2y_{1}-y_{2}-x_{2} and H2=x2​y22−2​y2−y1−x1H_{2}=x_{2}y_{2}^{2}-2y_{2}-y_{1}-x_{1}. The vector HH is the mother code of the baby series vector (h1,h2)(h_{1},h_{2}) where h1h_{1} and h2h_{2} are related by h1=1−1+x2+h2h_{1}=1-\sqrt{1+x_{2}+h_{2}} and h2=(1−1+x2​(x1+h1))/x2h_{2}=(1-\sqrt{1+x_{2}(x_{1}+h_{1})})/x_{2}. The mother code HH defines the same baby series vector as the mother code H′=(H1′,H2′)H^{\prime}=(H^{\prime}_{1},H^{\prime}_{2}) given by

H1′=−x1+x23+2​x2−4​x2​y13+(3+4​x22)​y1+(−2​x22−2+4​x2)​y12+x2​y14H^{\prime}_{1}=-x_{1}+x_{2}^{3}+2x_{2}-4x_{2}y_{1}^{3}+(3+4x_{2}^{2})y_{1}+(-2x_{2}^{2}-2+4x_{2})y_{1}^{2}+x_{2}y_{1}^{4},

H2′=−y12+2​y1+y2+x2H^{\prime}_{2}=-y_{1}^{2}+2y_{1}+y_{2}+x_{2}.

Now, Dy​H′​(0,0)D_{y}H^{\prime}(0,0) is unipotent upper triangular and H1′H_{1}^{\prime} does not depend on y2y_{2}. Hence, the expansion of the series h1h_{1} can be computed up to a any order from the equation H1′=0H_{1}^{\prime}=0. From H2′=0H_{2}^{\prime}=0 we get h2=−x2−2​h1+h12h_{2}=-x_{2}-2h_{1}+h_{1}^{2}.

7. Construction of codes

Codes of algebraic power series as above were introduced by Alonso, Mora and Raimondo. Their construction is based on an effective version of the Artin-Mazur theorem [AM, p.÷ 88, AMR, appendix, BCR, Thm.÷ 8.4.4, p.÷ 173].

Theorem 7.1. For any algebraic series g∈K⁡[[x]]g\in K[[x]] there is a finite algorithm to construct from an algebraic relation P⁡(x,t)=0P(x,t)=0 satisfied by gg and the Taylor expansion of gg up to sufficiently high degree a family code (H,G)∈K​[x,y]p×K⁡[x,y](H,G)\in K[x,y]^{p}\times K[x,y] of gg, for some pp.

Proof. Let P⁡(x,g⁡(x))=0P(x,g(x))=0 be a minimal hence irreducible algebraic relation for gg. Denote by X⊆𝔸Kn+1X\subseteq{{{\tenmsb A}}}_{K}^{n+1} the zero-set of PP in affine (n+1)(n+1)-space 𝔸Kn+1{{{\tenmsb A}}}_{K}^{n+1} over KK. We assume that g⁡(0)=0g(0)=0 so that (0,0)∈X(0,0)\in X. Let YY be the normalization of XX. Choose an embedding Y⊂𝔸n+pY\subset{{{\tenmsb A}}}^{n+p} so that the normalization map π:Y→X\pi:Y\rightarrow X is induced by the projection 𝔸n+p→𝔸n+1{{{\tenmsb A}}}^{n+p}\rightarrow{{{\tenmsb A}}}^{n+1}, (x,y)→(x,y1)(x,y)\rightarrow(x,y_{1}) on the first n+1n+1 components.

The Taylor expansion of gg specifies a unique point b∈Yb\in Y which maps to 0∈X0\in X and through which, by the universal property of normalization, passes a lifting (x,g~​(x))(x,\mathaccent 869{g}(x)) of (x,g⁡(x))(x,g(x)). From Zariski’s Main Theorem [Za, Mu, p.÷ 209] we know that YY is analytically irrreducible at bb. But as YY contains the graph of g~\mathaccent 869{g} and has dimension nn, it is smooth at bb. By the Jacobian criterion it is therefore possible to choose polynomial equations H1,…,HpH_{1},\ldots,H_{p} defining YY in a Zariski neighborhood of bb in 𝔸n+p{{{\tenmsb A}}}^{n+p} and satisfying at bb the assumption of the implicit function theorem, i.e., of a mother code. Let (h1,…,hp)(h_{1},\ldots,h_{p}) be the associated baby series vector. By the special choice of π\pi we get g=h1g=h_{1}, say g=G⁡(h1,…,hp)g=G(h_{1},\ldots,h_{p}) with father code G=y1G=y_{1}. This proves the theorem.

The construction of the normalization is effective [dJP] and implemented for instance in the computer-algebra program Singular [GPS].

When handling several algebraic power series it is more economic to work with one mother code and several father codes instead of choosing separate mother codes for each series. This goes as follows.

Let be given mother codes Hj∈K​[x,yj]pjH^{j}\in K[x,y^{j}]^{p_{j}} for j=1,…,rj=1,\ldots,r in distinct sets of variables yj=(y1j,…,ypjj)y^{j}=(y_{1}^{j},\ldots,y_{p_{j}}^{j}) defining baby series vector hj=(h1j,…,hpjj)∈K​[[x]]pjh^{j}=(h_{1}^{j},\ldots,h_{p_{j}}^{j})\in K[[x]]^{p_{j}}. The direct sum HH of the HjH^{j}’s is given as the row vector H=(H1,…,Hr)∈Πj=1r​K​[x,y]pj≅K​[x,y]pH=(H^{1},\ldots,H^{r})\in\Pi_{j=1}^{r}K[x,y]^{p_{j}}\cong K[x,y]^{p}, where yy denotes the collection of all yjy^{j} and p=∑pjp=\sum p_{j}. This HH is again a mother code, because the Jacobian matrix Dy​H​(0,0)D_{y}H(0,0) of HH with respect to yy at 00 has block diagonal form with invertible blocks equal to Dyj​Hj​(0,0)D_{y^{j}}H^{j}(0,0) on the diagonal. The vector h=(h1,…,hr)h=(h^{1},\ldots,h^{r}) obtained by listing all baby series vectors hjh^{j} of the mother codes HjH^{j} in a row is the baby series vector of HH. This passage to direct sums of mother codes allows us to treat several baby series vectors hjh^{j} simultaneously as one baby series vector hh (with many components). Accordingly, finitely many algebraic series can always be considered as produced by certain father codes from the same baby series vector h=(h1,…,hp)h=(h_{1},\ldots,h_{p}) of one mother code H∈K​[x,y]pH\in K[x,y]^{p}. This allows us to work throughout with vectors in K​[x,h1,…,hp]sK[x,h_{1},\ldots,h_{p}]^{s}.

Note that mother codes as defined above may require large sets of variables and are thus computationally very expensive.

8. Codes for modules of algebraic series

Let be given algebraic power series vectors g1,…,gr∈K​[[x]]sg_{1},\ldots,g_{r}\in K[[x]]^{s} vanishing at 00 with mother code H∈K​[x,y]pH\in K[x,y]^{p}, baby series vector h∈K​[[x]]ph\in K[[x]]^{p} and father code G∈K​[x,y]s×rG\in K[x,y]^{s\times r} so that gk=Gk​(x,h⁡(x))g_{k}=G_{k}(x,h(x)). The submodule ⟨gk⟩\langle g_{k}\rangle of K​[[x]]sK[[x]]^{s} generated by the series gkg_{k} admits the following polynomial description.

Lemma 8.1. Let ⟨(yi−hi)⋅eℓ,gk⟩\langle(y_{i}-h_{i})\cdot e_{\ell},g_{k}\rangle and ⟨Hi⋅eℓ,Gk⟩\langle H_{i}\cdot e_{\ell},G_{k}\rangle be the submodules of K​[[x,y]]sK[[x,y]]^{s} generated by the vectors (yi−hi)⋅eℓ(y_{i}-h_{i})\cdot e_{\ell} and gkg_{k}, respectively Hi⋅eℓH_{i}\cdot e_{\ell} and GkG_{k}, for 1≤i≤p1\leq i\leq p, 1≤ℓ≤s1\leq\ell\leq s, 1≤k≤r1\leq k\leq r. Then

⟨(yi−hi)⋅eℓ,gk⟩=⟨Hi⋅eℓ,Gk⟩\langle(y_{i}-h_{i})\cdot e_{\ell},g_{k}\rangle\,=\,\langle H_{i}\cdot e_{\ell},G_{k}\rangle.

Proof. We fix a monomial order <η<_{\eta} on ℕn×{1,…,s}{{{\tenmsb N}}}^{n}\times\{1,\ldots,s\} and choose an extension <ε<_{\varepsilon} of <η<_{\eta} to ℕn+p×{1,…,s}{{{\tenmsb N}}}^{n+p}\times\{1,\ldots,s\} which is degree compatible with respect to ℕp{{{\tenmsb N}}}^{p} and satisfies yi⋅eℓ<εxj⋅eℓy_{i}\cdot e_{\ell}<_{\varepsilon}x_{j}\cdot e_{\ell} for all 1≤i≤p1\leq i\leq p, 1≤j≤n1\leq j\leq n and 1≤ℓ≤s1\leq\ell\leq s. After a suitable multiplication of HH with a constant matrix in GLp​(K){\rm GL}_{p}(K) we may assume that in⁡(Hi⋅eℓ)=yi⋅eℓ{\rm in}(H_{i}\cdot e_{\ell})=y_{i}\cdot e_{\ell}.

The ideal ⟨Hi⟩\langle H_{i}\rangle of K⁡[[x,y]]K[[x,y]] generated by H1,…,HpH_{1},\ldots,H_{p} is contained in the ideal ⟨yi−hi⟩\langle y_{i}-h_{i}\rangle because of H⁡(x,h⁡(x))=0H(x,h(x))=0. Take a monomial order <δ<_{\delta} on ℕn+p{{{\tenmsb N}}}^{n+p} so that yi<δxjy_{i}<_{\delta}x_{j} for all 1≤i≤p1\leq i\leq p and 1≤j≤n1\leq j\leq n. The initial ideals of ⟨Hi⟩\langle H_{i}\rangle and ⟨yi−hi⟩\langle y_{i}-h_{i}\rangle coincide because, by the choice of <δ<_{\delta}, they are both generated by y1,…,ypy_{1},\ldots,y_{p}. By the Division Theorem for formal power series, the two ideals coincide. As gkg_{k} is obtained from GkG_{k} by replacing yiy_{i} by hih_{i}, the submodules of K​[[x,y]]sK[[x,y]]^{s} generated by g1,…,grg_{1},\ldots,g_{r}, respectively G1,…,GrG_{1},\ldots,G_{r} are congruent modulo ⟨yi−hi⟩=⟨Hi⟩\langle y_{i}-h_{i}\rangle\,=\,\langle H_{i}\rangle. This proves the lemma.

We call I~=⟨Hi⋅eℓ,Gk⟩⊂K​[[x,y]]s\mathaccent 869{I}=\,\langle H_{i}\cdot e_{\ell},G_{k}\rangle\,\subset K[[x,y]]^{s}, or, more accurately, its polynomial generators Hi⋅eℓH_{i}\cdot e_{\ell} and GkG_{k}, the family code of the submodule I=⟨gk⟩I=\,\langle g_{k}\rangle of K​[[x]]sK[[x]]^{s}. Observe that I~∩K​[[x]]s=I\mathaccent 869{I}\cap K[[x]]^{s}=I.

Lemma 8.2. Let be given a monomial order <η<_{\eta} on ℕn×{1,…,s}{{{\tenmsb N}}}^{n}\times\{1,\ldots,s\} and an extension <ε<_{\varepsilon} of <η<_{\eta} to ℕn+p×{1,…,s}{{{\tenmsb N}}}^{n+p}\times\{1,\ldots,s\} which is degree compatible with respect to ℕp{{{\tenmsb N}}}^{p} and satisfies yi⋅eℓ<εxj⋅eℓy_{i}\cdot e_{\ell}<_{\varepsilon}x_{j}\cdot e_{\ell} for all 1≤i≤p1\leq i\leq p, 1≤j≤n1\leq j\leq n and 1≤ℓ≤s1\leq\ell\leq s. Let I~=⟨Hi⋅eℓ,Gk⟩\mathaccent 869{I}=\,\langle H_{i}\cdot e_{\ell},G_{k}\rangle and I=⟨gk⟩I=\,\langle g_{k}\rangle be the respective submodules of K​[[x,y]]sK[[x,y]]^{s} and K​[[x]]sK[[x]]^{s}. Then

in⁡(I~)∩K​[[x]]s=in⁡(I){\rm in}(\mathaccent 869{I})\cap K[[x]]^{s}={\rm in}(I).

Proof. We may choose a minimal reduced standard basis of I~\mathaccent 869{I}. Let g~k\mathaccent 869{g}_{k} be an element of this basis which does not have an initial monomial vector of the form yi⋅eℓy_{i}\cdot e_{\ell}. From reducedness it follows that g~k\mathaccent 869{g}_{k} is independent of y1,…,ypy_{1},\ldots,y_{p}, say g~k∈I~∩K​[[x]]s=I\mathaccent 869{g}_{k}\in\mathaccent 869{I}\cap K[[x]]^{s}=I. In particular, the vectors g~k\mathaccent 869{g}_{k} form a standard basis of II and hence in⁡(I~)∩K​[[x]]s=in⁡(I){\rm in}(\mathaccent 869{I})\cap K[[x]]^{s}={\rm in}(I).

9. Construction of standard basis

The first construction we need is a direct consequence of Mora’s tangent cone algorithm [Mo], respectively Lazard’s homogenization method [Lz], cf.÷ also with [AMR, Thm.÷ 1.3, CLO, p.÷ 202, Gr1, Gr2, GP, Thm.÷ 6.4.3]. It provides an algorithm to construct the family code of a (not necessarily reduced) standard basis of a module of algebraic power series vectors.

Theorem 9.1. Let II be a submodule of K​[[x]]sK[[x]]^{s} generated by algebraic power series vectors g1,…,gr∈K​[[x]]sg_{1},\ldots,g_{r}\in K[[x]]^{s} which are given by their family code. Let be chosen a monomial order <η<_{\eta} on ℕn×{1,…,s}{{{\tenmsb N}}}^{n}\times\{1,\ldots,s\}. There is a finite algorithm to compute the family codes of the elements of a standard basis of II with respect to <η<_{\eta} from the family codes of g1,…,grg_{1},\ldots,g_{r}. In particular, it is possible to compute the initial module in⁡(I){\rm in}(I) of II.

Proof. Let g1,…,grg_{1},\ldots,g_{r} have mother code H∈K​[x,y]pH\in K[x,y]^{p}, baby series vector h∈K​[[x]]ph\in K[[x]]^{p} and father code G∈K​[x,y]s×rG\in K[x,y]^{s\times r}. Extend <η<_{\eta} to a monomial order <ε<_{\varepsilon} on ℕn+p×{1,…,s}{{{\tenmsb N}}}^{n+p}\times\{1,\ldots,s\} which is degree compatible with respect to ℕp{{{\tenmsb N}}}^{p} and satisfies yi⋅eℓ<εxj⋅eℓy_{i}\cdot e_{\ell}<_{\varepsilon}x_{j}\cdot e_{\ell} for all ii, jj and ℓ\ell. We assume w.l.o.g. that the initial monomial vectors of Hi⋅eℓH_{i}\cdot e_{\ell} with respect to <ε<_{\varepsilon} are yi⋅eℓy_{i}\cdot e_{\ell}.

As I~=⟨Hi⋅eℓ,Gk⟩\mathaccent 869{I}=\,\langle H_{i}\cdot e_{\ell},G_{k}\rangle is generated by polynomial vectors, Mora’s tangent cone algorithm or Lazard’s homogenization method apply to construct a polynomial standard basis for it. This basis is in general not reduced. We may choose a minimal basis consisting of the vectors Hi⋅eℓH_{i}\cdot e_{\ell} with in⁡(Hi⋅eℓ)=yi⋅eℓ{\rm in}(H_{i}\cdot e_{\ell})=y_{i}\cdot e_{\ell} and of other polynomial vectors G~1,…,G~r′∈K​[x,y]s\mathaccent 869{G}_{1},\ldots,\mathaccent 869{G}_{r^{\prime}}\in K[x,y]^{s} with initial monomial vectors in K​[[x]]sK[[x]]^{s}. The latter form the father code of algebraic power series vectors g~1,…,g~r′∈K​[[x]]s\mathaccent 869{g}_{1},\ldots,\mathaccent 869{g}_{r^{\prime}}\in K[[x]]^{s}, say g~k=G~k​(x,h)\mathaccent 869{g}_{k}=\mathaccent 869{G}_{k}(x,h). Note that G~k\mathaccent 869{G}_{k} is congruent to gkg_{k} modulo the submodule ⟨Hi⋅eℓ⟩\langle H_{i}\cdot e_{\ell}\rangle of K​[[x]]sK[[x]]^{s}. By Lemma 8.2, the g~k\mathaccent 869{g}_{k} form a standard basis of II. This proves the theorem.

10. Construction of reduced standard basis

The central part in establishing the division algorithm for modules of algebraic power series vectors is the construction of a reduced standard basis. The mere existence follows from Hironaka’s theorem. The effective part in the special case of principal ideals, i.e., the construction of the code of the Weierstrass form of an xnx_{n}-regular algebraic power series, has been established by Alonso, Mora and Raimondo [AMR, Thm.÷ 5.5]. The general statement is as follows:

Theorem 10.1. Let II be a submodule of K​[[x]]sK[[x]]^{s} generated by algebraic power series vectors. Assume that II satisfies Hironaka’s box condition with respect to a monomial order <η<_{\eta} on ℕn×{1,…,s}{{{\tenmsb N}}}^{n}\times\{1,\ldots,s\}. Then the family codes of a reduced standard basis of II can be computed by a finite algorithm from the family codes of any algebraic power series vectors g1,…,gr∈K​[[x]]sg_{1},\ldots,g_{r}\in K[[x]]^{s} generating II.

The proof of this result is given in sections 13 to 15. In the formal power series case, a reduced standard basis can be constructed up to any given degree by dividing monomial generators of the initial module by the module itself. For algebraic series, this construction would require to dispose already of an effective division algorithm. To avoid this logical cycle, reduced standard bases have to be constructed in a different way.

The clue relies in the concept of a virtual reduced standard basis. Such a basis consists of polynomial vectors whose coefficients are unknown and written as new variables. Upon replacing the variables by suitable series in xx, the virtual reduced standard basis will transform into an actual reduced standard basis of the module. The resulting coefficient series of the actual reduced standard basis – more precisely, their codes – are computed by dividing the polynomial generators of the module ⟨(yi−hi)⋅eℓ,gk⟩=⟨Hi⋅eℓ,Gk⟩\langle(y_{i}-h_{i})\cdot e_{\ell},g_{k}\rangle\,=\,\langle H_{i}\cdot e_{\ell},G_{k}\rangle by the virtual basis using the polynomial division algorithm. The definition requires that both the generators and the virtual basis are polynomial vectors, and that the initial monomial vectors of the virtual reduced standard basis can be interpreted as the leading (i.e., maximal) monomial vectors w.r.t.÷ another, suitably chosen monomial order. The choice of this order is rather subtle, see section 13. The remainders of the division then allow us to extract the codes of the required coefficients series.

11. Effective division for algebraic power series

Our main result asserts that the division by modules of algebraic power series vectors with box condition can be made effective, i.e., can be performed by applying finitely many operations to the codes. The case of principal ideals II, say the effective Weierstrass Division Theorem for algebraic power series, is due to Alonso, Mora and Raimondo in [AMR, Thm.÷ 5.6].

Theorem 11.1. Let II be a submodule of K​[[x]]sK[[x]]^{s} generated by algebraic power series vectors. Assume that II satisfies Hironaka’s box condition with respect to a monomial order <η<_{\eta} on ℕn×{1,…,s}{{{\tenmsb N}}}^{n}\times\{1,\ldots,s\}. Let be given the family codes of algebraic power series vectors g1,…,gr∈K​[[x]]sg_{1},\ldots,g_{r}\in K[[x]]^{s} generating II. There exists a finite algorithm which computes, for any algebraic power series vector f∈K​[[x]]sf\in K[[x]]^{s}, from the family code of ff the family codes of algebraic power series a1,…,ara_{1},\ldots,a_{r} in K⁡[[x]]K[[x]] and of an algebraic power series vector c∈co⁡(I)⊂K​[[x]]sc\in{\rm co}(I)\subset K[[x]]^{s} so that

f=∑k=1rak​gk+cf=\sum_{k=1}^{r}a_{k}g_{k}+c

is a formal power series division of ff by g1,…,grg_{1},\ldots,g_{r}.

The algorithm produces quotients aka_{k} which are algebraic series but which in general need not satisfy the support conditions of the formal power series division as in [Ga]. The remainder cc, of course, is unique and only depends on the chosen monomial order <η<_{\eta}.

We shall prove Theorem 11.1 by first constructing from g1,…,grg_{1},\ldots,g_{r} via Theorems 9.1 and 10.1 the family codes of a reduced standard basis of II. The division algorithm for a reduced standard basis will then be established by induction on the number of variables.

12. Logical structure of the proofs of Theorems 10.1 and 11.1

Both theorems will be established independently of Hironaka’s existential division theorem. We start with establishing Theorem 10.1, the construction of the codes of a reduced standard basis, in the special case of xnx_{n}-regular modules. This is the hardest part of the whole story. It relies on introducing the virtual reduced standard basis of the module, which allows us to perform polynomial divisions for constructing the required codes. This section is inspired by Mora’s tangent cone algorithm and the techniques of Alonso, Mora and Raimondo in [AMR]. Extracting from the virtual reduced standard basis the actual reduced standard basis uses in an essential way the assumption of xnx_{n}-regularity.

From Theorem 10.1 for xnx_{n}-regular modules we deduce the division algorithm of Theorem 11.1 for xnx_{n}-regular modules. The algorithm uses again a polynomial division, this time by the codes of the reduced standard basis. For its termination it is necessary that the basis is already reduced.

The general cases of Theorems 10.1 and 11.1 are then deduced simultaneously from the special cases by induction on the number of variables and using Hironaka’s box condition together with the notion of Janet basis. One selects from the given (not yet reduced) standard basis of the module those elements which are xnx_{n}-regular. Such elements exist because of the box condition. Considering the module generated by these elements, one may construct the codes of its reduced standard basis via Theorem 10.1 in the special case. Then Theorem 11.1 allows us to reduce effectively the remaining elements with respect to the first set of elements. By induction on the number of variables, the tails of the first elements can now be divided conversely by the remaining elements, yielding eventually the codes of the whole reduced standard basis of the module. Once this is achieved, it is relatively simple to establish also the division of Theorem 11.1 in the general case.

13. Proof of Theorem 10.1 for xnx_{n}-regular modules

In the situation of Theorem 10.1, we first treat the case where II is xnx_{n}-regular with respect to <η<_{\eta}. As seen in Lemmata 8.1 and 8.2, it suffices to construct the family code of a reduced standard basis of the submodule I~=⟨Hi⋅eℓ,Gk⟩=⟨(yi−hi)⋅eℓ,gk⟩\mathaccent 869{I}=\,\langle H_{i}\cdot e_{\ell},G_{k}\rangle\,=\,\langle(y_{i}-h_{i})\cdot e_{\ell},g_{k}\rangle of K​[[x,y]]sK[[x,y]]^{s} with respect to the chosen extension <ε<_{\varepsilon} of <η<_{\eta}. Note here that I~\mathaccent 869{I} is not xnx_{n}-regular, since also the yi⋅eℓy_{i}\cdot e_{\ell} appear in the initial module. This is, however, not a serious drawback. The proof is somewhat involved and goes in several steps. Let us first specify the setting.

(a) We suppose that the generators gkg_{k} of II vanish at 00 for all 1≤k≤r1\leq k\leq r. Hence this also holds for all Hi⋅eℓH_{i}\cdot e_{\ell} and GkG_{k}. We may assume by Theorem 9.1 and its proof that the polynomial vectors Hi⋅eℓH_{i}\cdot e_{\ell} and GkG_{k} form a minimal standard basis of I~\mathaccent 869{I}. Hence r≤sr\leq s. The canonical direct monomial complement co⁡(I~){\rm co}(\mathaccent 869{I}) of in⁡(I~){\rm in}(\mathaccent 869{I}) in K​[[x,y]]sK[[x,y]]^{s} is of form

co(I~)=⊕m=1r⊕j=0dm−1K[[x′]]⋅xnj⋅em⊕⊕m=r+1sK[[x]]⋅em{\rm co}(\mathaccent 869{I})=\oplus_{m=1}^{r}\,\oplus_{j=0}^{d_{m}-1}K[[x^{\prime}]]\cdot x_{n}^{j}\cdot e_{m}\,\,\oplus\,\,\oplus_{m=r+1}^{s}\,K[[x]]\cdot e_{m}.

Write a reduced standard basis of I~\mathaccent 869{I} as

bi​ℓ=yi⋅eℓ−bi​ℓ∘−∑m=1r∑j=0dm−1ui​ℓ​m​j​(x′)⋅xnj⋅em−∑m=r+1svi​ℓ​m​(x)⋅emb_{i\ell}=y_{i}\cdot e_{\ell}-b_{i\ell}^{\circ}-\sum_{m=1}^{r}\sum_{j=0}^{d_{m}-1}u_{i\ell mj}(x^{\prime})\cdot x_{n}^{j}\cdot e_{m}-\sum_{m=r+1}^{s}v_{i\ell m}(x)\cdot e_{m},

bk=xndk⋅ek−bk∘−∑m=1r∑j=0dm−1uk​m​j​(x′)⋅xnj⋅em−∑m=r+1svk​m​(x)⋅emb_{k}=x_{n}^{d_{k}}\cdot e_{k}-b_{k}^{\circ}-\sum_{m=1}^{r}\sum_{j=0}^{d_{m}-1}u_{kmj}(x^{\prime})\cdot x_{n}^{j}\cdot e_{m}-\sum_{m=r+1}^{s}v_{km}(x)\cdot e_{m},

with polynomial vectors bi​ℓ∘b_{i\ell}^{\circ} and bk∘b_{k}^{\circ} in

⊕m=1r⊕j=0dm−1Kxnj⋅em⊕⊕m=r+1sK⋅em\oplus_{m=1}^{r}\,\oplus_{j=0}^{d_{m}-1}Kx_{n}^{j}\cdot e_{m}\,\,\oplus\,\,\oplus_{m=r+1}^{s}\,K\cdot e_{m}

and power series ui​ℓ​m​j​(x′)u_{i\ell mj}(x^{\prime}), vi​ℓ​m​(x)v_{i\ell m}(x), uk​m​j​(x′)u_{kmj}(x^{\prime}) and vk​m​(x)v_{km}(x) vanishing at 00. In particular, these vectors have zero entries in the last s−rs-r components. Since inε​(bi​ℓ)=yi⋅eℓ{\rm in}_{\varepsilon}(b_{i\ell})=y_{i}\cdot e_{\ell} and inε​(bk)=xndk⋅ek{\rm in}_{\varepsilon}(b_{k})=x_{n}^{d_{k}}\cdot e_{k} the ℓ\ell-th component of bi​ℓ∘b_{i\ell}^{\circ} and the kk-th component of bk∘b_{k}^{\circ} are both zero.

The series bi​ℓb_{i\ell} have different shapes according to whether 1≤ℓ≤r1\leq\ell\leq r or r+1≤ℓ≤sr+1\leq\ell\leq s. Namely, for r+1≤ℓ≤sr+1\leq\ell\leq s, it follows from the xnx_{n}-regularity of II that the vectors (yi−hi)⋅eℓ(y_{i}-h_{i})\cdot e_{\ell} are already reduced. Hence we have bi​ℓ=(yi−hi)⋅eℓb_{i\ell}=(y_{i}-h_{i})\cdot e_{\ell} for r+1≤ℓ≤sr+1\leq\ell\leq s. This will be used later on. We are grateful to D.÷ Wagner for specifying an inaccuracy which appeared at this place in an earlier draft of the paper.

In a first step, we determine the vectors bi​ℓ∘b_{i\ell}^{\circ} and bk∘b_{k}^{\circ}. Afterwards, the family codes of the coefficient series ui​ℓ​m​j​(x′)u_{i\ell mj}(x^{\prime}), vi​ℓ​m​(x)v_{i\ell m}(x), uk​m​j​(x′)u_{kmj}(x^{\prime}) and vk​m​(x)v_{km}(x) will be constructed. This will show in particular that they are algebraic series.

(b) In order to compute bi​ℓ∘b_{i\ell}^{\circ} and bk∘b_{k}^{\circ}, one can construct the reduced standard basis of I~\mathaccent 869{I} up to a sufficiently high degree by applying its formal power series construction modulo a sufficiently high power of the maximal ideal of K⁡[[x,y]]K[[x,y]].

(c) The series ui​ℓ​m​j​(x′)u_{i\ell mj}(x^{\prime}), vi​ℓ​m​(x)v_{i\ell m}(x), uk​m​j​(x′)u_{kmj}(x^{\prime}) and vk​m​(x)v_{km}(x) will be determined by a trick which has already appeared in the literature, see e.g.÷ [AMR]: Define the virtual reduced standard basis of I~\mathaccent 869{I} as the polynomial vectors

We have noticed above that, for r+1≤ℓ≤sr+1\leq\ell\leq s, the vectors bi​ℓb_{i\ell} equal (yi−hi)⋅eℓ(y_{i}-h_{i})\cdot e_{\ell}. As the polynomial vectors Bi​ℓB_{i\ell} are the father codes of bi​ℓb_{i\ell} they will therefore have, for r+1≤ℓ≤sr+1\leq\ell\leq s, only one non-zero entry, namely in the ℓ\ell’s component. (e) We show that UU and VV have no constant terms. Replacing in Ri​ℓR_{i\ell} and RkR_{k} the variables uu and vv by the series u⁡(x′)u(x^{\prime}) and v⁡(x)v(x) produces power series vectors ri​ℓr_{i\ell} and rkr_{k} which belong to co⁡(I~){\rm co}(\mathaccent 869{I}) because u⁡(x′)u(x^{\prime}) does not depend on xnx_{n} and UU does not depend on vv. As u⁡(x′)u(x^{\prime}) and v⁡(x)v(x) have no constant term, also UU and VV have no constant term.
