15. Proofs of Theorems 10.1 and 11.1 in the general case

The idea for proving both theorems in the general case is to split a given minimal standard basis of II into two groups specified by the variables appearing in their initial monomial vectors. The first group consists of generators whose initial monomial vectors are pure xnx_{n}-powers. The remaining generators have initial monomial vectors which involve also some other variable.

So let be given, by Theorem 9.1, vectors g1,…,grg_{1},\ldots,g_{r} which form a minimal standard basis of II. Adding suitable monomial multiples of the gkg_{k} we may assume that g1,…,grg_{1},\ldots,g_{r} form a minimal Janet basis of II with scopes n1,…,nrn_{1},\ldots,n_{r}. We order g1,…,grg_{1},\ldots,g_{r} and permute the components of K​[[x]]sK[[x]]^{s} so that, for some 1≤t≤r1\leq t\leq r, the vectors g1,…,gtg_{1},\ldots,g_{t} are xnx_{n}-regular with initial monomial vectors xndk⋅ekx_{n}^{d_{k}}\cdot e_{k}, and so that the initial monomial vectors of the remaining gt+1,…,grg_{t+1},\ldots,g_{r} involve at least one of the variables x1,…,xn−1x_{1},\ldots,x_{n-1}. It is easy to see that the scopes nt+1,…,nrn_{t+1},\ldots,n_{r} of gt+1,…,grg_{t+1},\ldots,g_{r} are all <n<n. This implies that

I=∑k=1tK⁡[[x]]⋅gk+∑k=t+1rK⁡[[x′]]⋅gkI=\sum_{k=1}^{t}K[[x]]\cdot g_{k}+\sum_{k=t+1}^{r}K[[x^{\prime}]]\cdot g_{k}.

Therefore no gt+1,…,grg_{t+1},\ldots,g_{r} need to be multiplied in the subsequent divisions by xnx_{n}.

By Theorem 10.1 in the xnx_{n}-regular case we may assume that g1,…,gtg_{1},\ldots,g_{t} form already a reduced standard basis of the submodule I0=⟨g1,…,gt⟩I_{0}=\,\langle g_{1},\ldots,g_{t}\rangle of K​[[x]]sK[[x]]^{s}. By Theorem 11.1 in the xnx_{n}-regular case we know how to divide gt+1,…,grg_{t+1},\ldots,g_{r} by g1,…,gtg_{1},\ldots,g_{t} through a finite algorithm for the respective family codes. This allows us to assume that gt+1,…,grg_{t+1},\ldots,g_{r} belong to

M=co⁡(I0)=∑m=1t∑j=0dm−1K⁡[[x′]]⋅xnj⋅em+∑m=t+1sK⁡[[x]]⋅emM={\rm co}(I_{0})=\sum_{m=1}^{t}\sum_{j=0}^{d_{m}-1}K[[x^{\prime}]]\cdot x_{n}^{j}\cdot e_{m}+\sum_{m=t+1}^{s}K[[x]]\cdot e_{m}.

It follows from the box condition that the initial monomial vectors of gt+1,…,grg_{t+1},\ldots,g_{r} have their non-zero entry in the first summand

M1=∑m=1t∑j=0dm−1K⁡[[x′]]⋅xnj⋅emM_{1}=\sum_{m=1}^{t}\sum_{j=0}^{d_{m}-1}K[[x^{\prime}]]\cdot x_{n}^{j}\cdot e_{m}

of MM. Setting I′=∑k=t+1rK⁡[[x′]]⋅gkI^{\prime}=\sum_{k=t+1}^{r}K[[x^{\prime}]]\cdot g_{k} we have I′⊂MI^{\prime}\subset M and in⁡(I′)⊂M1{\rm in}(I^{\prime})\subset M_{1}. The monomial order on ℕn×{1,…,s}{{{\tenmsb N}}}^{n}\times\{1,\ldots,s\} induces via the inclusion M⊂K​[[x]]sM\subset K[[x]]^{s} in a natural way an ordering of the monomial vectors in MM.

We may now apply induction on nn as follows.

First notice that in⁡(I′){\rm in}(I^{\prime}), as a submodule of the free finite K⁡[[x′]]K[[x^{\prime}]]-module M1M_{1}, satisfies again Hironaka’s box condition with respect to the induced ordering of the variables. Secondly, no division occurs in the second summand M2=∑m=t+1sK⁡[[x]]⋅emM_{2}=\sum_{m=t+1}^{s}K[[x]]\cdot e_{m} of MM. Therefore, by induction on the number of variables and discarding the (irrelevant) fact that the summand M2M_{2} is not finitely generated as K⁡[[x′]]K[[x^{\prime}]]-module, we may assume to know how to construct the reduced standard basis of the K⁡[[x′]]K[[x^{\prime}]]-submodule I′I^{\prime} of MM by a finite algorithm on the level of codes. Notice that this basis, when considered as vectors in K​[[x]]sK[[x]]^{s}, remains reduced with respect to g1,…,gtg_{1},\ldots,g_{t} because its elements belong to M=co⁡(I0)M={\rm co}(I_{0}).

So we may assume that gt+1,…,grg_{t+1},\ldots,g_{r} already form a reduced standard basis of I′I^{\prime}. By induction on nn we may apply the division algorithm of Theorem 11.1 to I′I^{\prime} as a submodule of MM. Thus we know how to divide effectively algebraic power series vectors in MM by I′I^{\prime}.

Apply this to the tails g¯k=xndk⋅ek−gk\overline{g}_{k}=x_{n}^{d_{k}}\cdot e_{k}-g_{k} of g1,…,gtg_{1},\ldots,g_{t}. They belong to MM since g1,…,gtg_{1},\ldots,g_{t} are a reduced standard basis of I0I_{0} and M=co⁡(I0)M={\rm co}(I_{0}). We divide these g¯k\overline{g}_{k} by I′I^{\prime}. This allows us to assume from the beginning that g1,…,gtg_{1},\ldots,g_{t} are reduced with respect to gt+1,…,grg_{t+1},\ldots,g_{r}, i.e., that g¯k∈co⁡(I′)\overline{g}_{k}\in{\rm co}(I^{\prime}) for 1≤k≤t1\leq k\leq t. As I′⊂M=co⁡(I0)I^{\prime}\subset M={\rm co}(I_{0}), the new g1,…,gtg_{1},\ldots,g_{t} form again a reduced standard basis (the module they generate may be different from I0I_{0}, but its initial module is the same). In total, we have found the reduced standard basis g1,…,grg_{1},\ldots,g_{r} of II. This proves Theorem 10.1.

As for Theorem 11.1, any algebraic power series vector f∈K​[[x]]sf\in K[[x]]^{s} we wish to divide by I=⟨g1,…,gr⟩I=\,\langle g_{1},\ldots,g_{r}\rangle can first be divided by I0=⟨g1,…,gt⟩I_{0}=\,\langle g_{1},\ldots,g_{t}\rangle using Theorem 11.1 in the xnx_{n}-regular case. It thus yields a remainder in M=co⁡(I0)M={\rm co}(I_{0}). Then, using induction on nn and that I′I^{\prime} satisfies the box condition in MM, we may divide this remainder as vector in MM by I′I^{\prime}. The resulting remainder can be interpreted, via the inclusion of MM in K​[[x]]sK[[x]]^{s}, as a vector in co⁡(I)⊂K​[[x]]s{\rm co}(I)\subset K[[x]]^{s}. It will coincide with the remainder of the formal power series division of ff by II in K​[[x]]sK[[x]]^{s}. It does not matter here that the second summand ∑m=t+1sK⁡[[x]]⋅em\sum_{m=t+1}^{s}K[[x]]\cdot e_{m} of MM is not finitely generated as K⁡[[x′]]K[[x^{\prime}]]-module, because no division occurs in the last s−rs-r components of ff.

This establishes the division algorithm for algebraic power series vectors ff in K​[[x]]sK[[x]]^{s} by submodules II with box condition. Theorem 11.1 is proven.

16. Example

In this section we show in a concrete situation how the algorithms of Theorem 10.1 and 11.1 work in practice (for more examples, see [Wa]). We will consider an ideal in three variables generated by algebraic power series involving a single baby series. Our objective will be the computation of the codes of the reduced standard basis of the ideal. As it will turn out, the reduced standard basis will consist of polynomials, so that, at the end, there will be no mother codes needed and the father codes of the basis coincide with the elements of the basis. Nevertheless, the example is significant, since it is not at all clear how to construct the codes of the reduced standard basis without using the techniques developed in the paper.

The example is chosen so as to illustrate the various aspects of the algorithm (reduction, division, passage to vectors, induction on the number of variables). Some steps could also be performed directly using some ad hoc tricks due to the simplicity of some of the generators of the ideals and modules involved. This will be indicated correspondingly. Nevertherless, all portions of the algorithm will show off at least once.

As a general rule, each step in the computations below will be followed by a renaming of the involved objects so as to keep the presentation as systematic as possible. In the subsequent step, letters will always refer to this renamed object and not to the original object defined at earlier stages of the exposition.

The initial variables will be denoted xx, yy and zz, corresponding to x1x_{1}, x2x_{2} and x3x_{3} in the text, with this ordering. This will affect xnx_{n}-regularity, being here first zz-regularity, then, later, yy-regularity and finally xx-regularity. Also, the involved polynomial divisions will use this ordering of the variables.

The additional auxiliary variables appearing in the mother codes will be denoted by t1t_{1}, t2t_{2}, …\ldots (instead of y1y_{1}, y2y_{2}, …\ldots as in the text). The respective baby series will be h1h_{1}, h2h_{2}, …\ldots

We consider the ideal II in K⁡[[x,y,z]]K[[x,y,z]] generated by three power series g1g_{1}, g2g_{2}, g3g_{3} given as

g1=z2+x​y​z+14​x​y​z2+…=g_{1}=z^{2}+xyz+{1\over 4}xyz^{2}+\ldots=

=z2+x​y​h​(z)=z^{2}+xyh(z),

g2=y​z+x2​z+y2​zg_{2}=yz+x^{2}z+y^{2}z,

g3=y2+x​y​zg_{3}=y^{2}+xyz.

Here,

h⁡(z)=1−1−z=12​z+18​z2+…h(z)=1-\sqrt{1-z}={1\over 2}z+{1\over 8}z^{2}+\ldots

is the only involved baby series. Its mother code HH is taken as

H=2​t−t2+zH=2t-t^{2}+z

(so that h=h⁡(z)h=h(z) is the unique formal power series solution of H⁡(z,t)=0H(z,t)=0 satisfying h⁡(0)=0h(0)=0.) Later on, when other mother codes will appear, we shall set t=t1t=t_{1}, h=h1h=h_{1} and H=H1H=H_{1}. The father codes of g1g_{1}, g2g_{2}, g3g_{3} are

G1=z2+x​y​tG_{1}=z^{2}+xyt

G2=y​z+x2​z+y2​zG_{2}=yz+x^{2}z+y^{2}z,

G3=y2+x​y​zG_{3}=y^{2}+xyz.

The last two G2G_{2} and G3G_{3} do not involve tt because g2g_{2} and g3g_{3} are polynomials and hence G2=g2G_{2}=g_{2} and G3=g3G_{3}=g_{3}. For our purposes it will be sufficient to have just one generator which is a true series.

We wish to compute the family codes of the reduced standard basis of I=⟨g1,g2,g3⟩⊂K⁡[[x,y,z]]I=\,\langle g_{1},g_{2},g_{3}\rangle\,\subset K[[x,y,z]] with respect to a given monomial order on ℕ3{{{\tenmsb N}}}^{3}. We shall choose the graded lexicographical order <η<_{\eta} on ℕ3{{{\tenmsb N}}}^{3} with x>y>zx>y>z. This yields the initial monomials

in⁡(g1)=z2{\rm in}(g_{1})=z^{2}

in⁡(g2)=y​z{\rm in}(g_{2})=yz,

in⁡(g3)=y2{\rm in}(g_{3})=y^{2}.

It will turn out these do not yet generate the initial ideal in⁡(I){\rm in}(I) of II. The missing monomial is x4​zx^{4}z, which is the initial monomial of the element

g4=x4​z−x3​y​z2+x4​y​h​(z)g_{4}=x^{4}z-x^{3}yz^{2}+x^{4}yh(z)

of II with father code

G4=x4​z−x3​y​z2+x4​y​tG_{4}=x^{4}z-x^{3}yz^{2}+x^{4}yt.

Actually, g1,…,g4g_{1},\ldots,g_{4} form a standard basis of II with respect to <η<_{\eta}. This basis is obviously not reduced.

Overview: For the convenience of the reader, let us list the various steps which will appear in the calculations (below, “computation of …” will always mean “computation of the code of …”.)

Step 1: Computation of a standard basis of II. In addition to g1g_{1}, g2g_{2}, g3g_{3} we will get a fourth generator g4g_{4} of II, the one from above.

Step 2: Specification of all xnx_{n}-regular elements of this basis and computation of the reduced standard basis of the ideal I1I_{1} generated by them. Here, xnx_{n} is zz; as only g1g_{1} is zz-regular, I1=⟨g1⟩I_{1}=\,\langle g_{1}\rangle is principal and its reduced standard basis can be computed with the algorithm of [AMR, Thm.÷ 5.5] or, equivalently, as described in Theorem 10.1 above in the xnx_{n}-regular case for principal ideals. The reduced standard basis of I1I_{1} will again be denoted by g1g_{1}. Its tail belongs to co⁡(I1)≅K​[[x,y]]2{\rm co}(I_{1})\cong K[[x,y]]^{2}, where co⁡(I1)=K⁡[[x,y]]⊕K⁡[[x,y]]​z{\rm co}(I_{1})=K[[x,y]]\oplus K[[x,y]]z denotes the canonical monomial direct complement of I1I_{1} in K⁡[[x,y,z]]K[[x,y,z]] with respect to the chosen monomial order.

Step 3: Reduction of g2g_{2}, g3g_{3}, g4g_{4} by I1=⟨g1⟩I_{1}=\,\langle g_{1}\rangle. This is the division of g2g_{2}, g3g_{3}, g4g_{4} by g1g_{1} with the algorithm of [AMR, Thm.÷ 5.6] or, equivalently, as described in Theorem 11.1 above in the xnx_{n}-regular case for principal ideals, xnx_{n} being here zz. The reduced series will again be denoted by g2g_{2}, g3g_{3}, g4g_{4}.

Step 4: Interpretation of g2g_{2}, g3g_{3}, g4g_{4} as vectors in co⁡(I1)≅K​[[x,y]]2{\rm co}(I_{1})\cong K[[x,y]]^{2} and computation of the reduced standard basis of the submodule I2=⟨g2,g3,g4⟩I_{2}=\,\langle g_{2},g_{3},g_{4}\rangle of K​[[x,y]]2K[[x,y]]^{2} generated by them. By Step 1, the vectors g2g_{2}, g3g_{3}, g4g_{4} already form a standard basis of I2I_{2}, so they need not be completed again. Step 4 consists of four substeps.

Substep 4A: Specification of all yy-regular elements among g2g_{2}, g3g_{3}, g4g_{4} and computation of the reduced standard basis of the submodule I3I_{3} of K​[[x,y]]2K[[x,y]]^{2} generated by these as described in Theorem 10.1 for the xnx_{n}-regular case (only g2g_{2} and g3g_{3} will be yy-regular, so that I3=⟨g2,g3⟩I_{3}=\,\langle g_{2},g_{3}\rangle.) The reduced standard basis of I3I_{3} will again be denoted by g2g_{2}, g3g_{3}. Its tails belong to co⁡(I3)≅K​[[x]]3{\rm co}(I_{3})\cong K[[x]]^{3}, where co⁡(I3)=(K⁡[[x]]⊕K⁡[[x]]​y)×K⁡[[x]]{\rm co}(I_{3})=(K[[x]]\oplus K[[x]]y)\times K[[x]] denotes the canonical monomial direct complement of I3I_{3} in K​[[x,y]]2K[[x,y]]^{2} with respect to the chosen monomial order.

Substep 4B: Reduction of g4g_{4} by I3=⟨g2,g3⟩I_{3}=\,\langle g_{2},g_{3}\rangle. This is the division of g4g_{4} by g2g_{2}, g3g_{3} in K​[[x,y]]2K[[x,y]]^{2} as described in Theorem 11.1 above in the xnx_{n}-regular case, xnx_{n} being now yy. The reduced vector will again be denoted by g4g_{4}.

Substep 4C: Interpretation of g4g_{4} as a vector in co⁡(I3)≅K​[[x]]3{\rm co}(I_{3})\cong K[[x]]^{3} and computation of the reduced standard basis of the submodule I4I_{4} of K​[[x]]3K[[x]]^{3} generated by it as described in Theorem 10.1 in the xnx_{n}-regular case, xnx_{n} being here xx. The situation will be so simple that the reduced standard basis of I4I_{4} can be read off directly without using Theorem 10.1. It will again be denoted by g4g_{4}.

Substep 4D: Reduction of g2g_{2}, g3g_{3} by I4=⟨g4⟩I_{4}=\,\langle g_{4}\rangle. Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.
